narrative:
The model estimated a 63.4% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above the risk threshold used for admission, your application was rejected; it is a risk estimate, not a certainty, and still implies about a one-in-three chance of passing.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile group (1), far below the accepted-student average near 6, and this factor pushed most strongly toward predicted failure. Your first-year standing also counted against you: you were in decile 2, again well below the accepted average of about 6, and this was the second-most influential factor toward failure. Your family income bracket, upper-middle, was the third-most important factor, but unlike the class-standing measures it worked slightly in your favor, nudging the prediction toward passing; it was not enough to offset the academic signals.

To improve your chances, address the academic concerns directly: speak with admissions or pre-law advising about how to strengthen your record, consider whether retaking the LSAT or additional coursework could demonstrate readiness, and prepare a clear explanation of any circumstances behind your early grades. Reapplication should focus on showing sustained academic improvement and a realistic bar-exam readiness plan.
